summary.big_en: Each substance has its own melting point and boiling point — that is how we tell substances apart.

glossary.def: Something about a substance that allows us to tell it apart from other substances.
glossary.example: Each substance has its own melting point (p.36).

glossary.def: The temperature at which a solid becomes a liquid.
glossary.example: Ice melts at 0 °C; the melting point of gold is 1064 °C (p.36).

glossary.def: The temperature at which particles throughout a liquid have enough energy to change to a gas.
glossary.example: Pure water boils at 100 °C, vinegar at 118 °C (p.36).

glossary.def: When particles on the surface of a liquid change into a gas.
glossary.example: Evaporation can occur at any temperature (p.36).

glossary.def: Everything that takes up space and has mass. Solid, liquid and gas are its three states.
glossary.example: Air is a mixture of gases, and gas is one of the states of matter (p.35, p.39).

points.t: Melting point is a property of a substance, so each substance has its own melting point (p.36).
Boiling point is a property too. Each substance boils at a certain temperature (p.36).
Boiling and evaporation both change a liquid into a gas, but they are not the same process (p.36).
All matter takes up space and has mass. Air is a mixture of gases, so air is matter (p.39).

checklists.title: Melting points in the book (p.36, p.62)
checklists.note: The Check your progress table (p.62) asks you to list these from highest to lowest.

rows.a: All the particles in the liquid
Most liquids boil only when heated

experiments.title: Measure and compare melting points
experiments.summary: The teacher heats three different solids in pans on a hotplate and measures the temperature of each one the moment it melts.
experiments.result: Each solid melts at a different temperature on the thermometer, and the readings go in a table.

experiments.title: Investigate the properties of gases
experiments.summary: Two blown-up balloons are hung from a ruler so they balance, then the tie on one balloon is loosened to let the air out.
experiments.result: When the tie on one balloon is loosened, the balanced ruler tips down on the side of the full balloon.

summary.big_en: Metals let heat and electricity pass through them. Glass and plastic do not.

glossary.def: Heat being transferred from one object to another.
glossary.example: A cold metal teaspoon in a hot cup of tea: the handle feels warm after a while (p.42-43).

glossary.def: A substance or material that conducts heat well.
glossary.example: Metals. Silver is the best conductor of heat (p.43-44).

glossary.def: A substance or material that is able to conduct electricity.
glossary.example: Metals, such as the copper connecting wire in the circuit (p.45).

glossary.def: A material or substance that is not a good conductor of electricity.
glossary.example: Plastic, rubber, glass and most non-metal substances (p.61).

points.t: Metals are good conductors of heat and silver is the best. Non-metals such as glass and plastic are not good conductors of heat (p.44).
How well a substance can conduct heat is a property of the substance. Some substances conduct heat better than others (p.44).
The ability to conduct electricity is a property of materials and substances. Metals conduct electricity (p.45).
Substances that are not good conductors of electricity are called insulators (p.61).

checklists.title: How well substances conduct — the book's table (p.47)
checklists.note: Measured in W/m−K. Question 4 asks you to find the measurements that do not fit the pattern.

experiments.title: Investigate how well different materials conduct heat
experiments.summary: A bead is stuck with petroleum jelly to the top of a metal spoon, a plastic spoon, a glass rod, a pencil and a piece of polystyrene foam, then all of them are stood in hot water.
experiments.result: The beads fall off one after another, and the order shows which material carried the heat fastest.

experiments.title: Investigate how well different substances conduct electricity
experiments.summary: A lamp circuit is set up with two free wire ends, and different substances (copper, steel, aluminium foil, graphite, sugar, water) are placed between the ends in turn.
experiments.result: For each substance the lamp is bright, dim or does not shine, recorded as two ticks, one tick or none.

summary.big_en: Some changes can be undone and some can never be undone.

glossary.def: A change that alters how a substance looks or feels, without turning it into a new substance.
glossary.example: A change of state, such as ice melting into water (p.50).

glossary.def: A change that can be changed back again.
glossary.example: Solid ice to liquid water, and liquid water back to solid ice (p.50).

glossary.def: A change that cannot be reversed.
glossary.example: Burning a match: the wood changes into a black substance called carbon (p.50).

glossary.def: The substance that dissolves.
glossary.example: The dissolved salt in sea water (p.51).

glossary.def: The substance in which the solute dissolves.
glossary.example: The water in sea water (p.51).

glossary.def: Looking the same throughout.
glossary.example: A solution has a uniform appearance, so you cannot see the solute in it (p.52).

glossary.def: How fast something happens.
glossary.example: Stirring increases the rate at which a solute dissolves (p.53).

points.t: A physical change alters how a substance looks or feels. The substance does not change into a new substance (p.50).
A change is reversible when the substance can be changed back to the way it was (p.50).
Irreversible changes cannot be reversed, and some turn one substance into another. That is a chemical change (p.50).
The solute and the solvent together form a solution. Sea water is salty because there is dissolved salt in the water (p.51).
When a solute dissolves, its particles move between the solvent particles and spread evenly. That is why you cannot see the solute afterwards (p.52).
Stirring increases the rate at which a solute dissolves. It spreads the solute particles into the spaces between the solvent particles more quickly (p.53).
In a heated solvent the particles gain energy and move faster, so the solute dissolves faster (p.54).

rows.b: Sometimes — then it is a chemical change

rows.a: Ice melts to water, water freezes to ice
rows.b: A burning match: wood becomes carbon

experiments.title: Getting started: ice cubes in the sun
experiments.summary: Ice cubes are left on a saucer in a warm place for five minutes, then the water is put back in the freezer.
experiments.result: After five minutes in the warm the ice has melted, and back in the freezer it becomes solid again.

experiments.title: Describe dissolving
experiments.summary: Look at the picture of copper sulfate being added to water and describe what happens to it.
experiments.result: The copper sulfate spreads through the water until you can no longer see it in the solution.

experiments.title: Does water temperature affect the rate of dissolving?
experiments.summary: A teaspoon of sugar is stirred into 100 ml of cold water and into 100 ml of hot water, and the time it takes to dissolve is measured for each.
experiments.result: The sugar in the hot water takes less time on the stopwatch than the sugar in the cold water.

summary.big_en: In a chemical reaction, substances react together and form a new substance.

glossary.def: When substances are mixed together, change, and form a new substance.
glossary.example: Vinegar mixed with bicarbonate of soda (p.57).

glossary.def: What substances do when they change together and form a new substance.
glossary.example: Vinegar and bicarbonate of soda react together (p.57).

glossary.def: The substances that react together.
glossary.example: Vinegar and bicarbonate of soda (p.57).

glossary.def: The new substances that form in a reaction.
glossary.example: The gas that is produced in the jar (p.57-58).

glossary.def: Something we can see that shows a product has formed.
glossary.example: The gas produced when vinegar and bicarbonate of soda react (p.58).

points.t: In a chemical reaction substances react together and form new substances. The substances that react are the reactants and the new ones are the products (p.57).
Sometimes we can see that a product has formed, and that is evidence of the reaction. There are also other ways to tell (p.58).
When clear limewater is mixed with carbon dioxide, the reaction forms a substance called calcium carbonate (p.59).

checklists.title: Three ways to tell a reaction has taken place (p.59 Q1)
checklists.note: Question 1 asks for three ways with an example of each; the topic's investigations show one each.

experiments.title: Identify reactants and products
experiments.summary: A teaspoon of bicarbonate of soda is added to vinegar in a jar and watched for five minutes.
experiments.result: A gas is produced straight away, and after five minutes you look for any other product.

experiments.title: Investigate evidence A — colour change and a new solid
experiments.summary: Iodine solution is added to water and cornstarch is stirred in; in another beaker, air is breathed through a straw into limewater.
experiments.result: Adding cornstarch to the iodine solution changes what you see, and breathing carbon dioxide into the limewater forms a new substance.

experiments.title: Investigate evidence B — temperature change
experiments.summary: Vinegar is poured over a ball of wire wool in a beaker, and the temperature is recorded straight away and again after five minutes.
experiments.result: The thermometer reading after five minutes is different from the reading taken at the start.

quiz.stem_en: At what temperature does ice melt?
quiz.why_en: Ice melts at 0 °C (p.36).

quiz.stem_en: What is the melting point of gold?
quiz.why_en: Gold melts at 1064 °C (p.36).

quiz.stem_en: From the Check your progress table, which substance has the LOWEST melting point?
quiz.why_en: Candle wax melts at 60 °C, the lowest in the table (p.62).

quiz.stem_en: Why is the melting point of a substance always lower than its boiling point?

choices.en: Because boiling needs less energy than melting
Because solids are hotter than liquids
Because melting only happens in an oven
Because a substance must be a liquid before it can boil

quiz.why_en: A solid melts into a liquid first; the liquid then needs more energy to boil (p.38 Q5).

quiz.stem_en: Pure water boils at 100 °C. At what temperature does vinegar boil?
quiz.why_en: Vinegar boils at 118 °C (p.36).

quiz.stem_en: What is the difference between boiling and evaporation?

choices.en: Boiling happens through the whole liquid; evaporation only at the surface
Boiling can happen at any temperature; evaporation needs heat

quiz.why_en: In boiling, all the particles gain enough energy; in evaporation only surface particles change to gas (p.36).

quiz.stem_en: Which of these can happen at any temperature, without heating?
quiz.why_en: Evaporation can occur at any temperature; most liquids boil only when heated (p.36).

quiz.stem_en: You heat 100 ml of water and 100 ml of vinegar on the same hotplate. Which boils first, and why?

choices.en: Vinegar — it has the lower boiling point
Water — it has the lower boiling point

quiz.why_en: Water boils at 100 °C, vinegar at 118 °C, so water reaches its boiling point first (p.36, p.38).

quiz.stem_en: Which TWO properties does the book say all matter has?

choices.en: It takes up space and it has mass
It is heavy and it is hot
It can be seen and it can be felt

quiz.why_en: All matter takes up space and has mass — including gases like air (p.39).

quiz.stem_en: Two balloons the same size hang from a balanced ruler. You let the air out of one. What happens?

choices.en: The ruler tips towards the full balloon
The ruler tips towards the empty balloon

quiz.why_en: The full balloon still has the mass of its air, so its side goes down (p.40).

quiz.stem_en: Why can't we usually feel the air around us?

choices.en: Because we only feel air when it is moving

quiz.why_en: "We can't feel air unless it is moving" (p.39). Air is still matter.

quiz.stem_en: A cold metal teaspoon is put into hot tea. After a while the handle feels warm. What is this called?
quiz.why_en: Heat is transferred along the spoon — conduction (p.42-43).

quiz.stem_en: Which substance does the book say is the best conductor of heat?
quiz.why_en: "Silver is the best conductor of heat" (p.44).

quiz.stem_en: In the bead investigation, why does the bead fall off the metal spoon first?

choices.en: Metal conducts heat best, so the jelly melts first
The bead was stuck on badly

quiz.why_en: Metal conducts heat fastest, melting the petroleum jelly first (p.43-44).

quiz.stem_en: In which cup will tea stay warm the longest?
quiz.why_en: Polystyrene foam is a poor conductor of heat, so heat stays in the tea (p.45 Q4).

quiz.stem_en: Why does food cook faster in the oven in a metal dish than in a glass dish?

choices.en: Metal conducts heat to the food faster than glass

quiz.why_en: Metal is a good thermal conductor; glass is not (p.62 Q2, p.44).

quiz.stem_en: From the book's table, which substance conducts electricity BEST?
quiz.why_en: Copper has the highest electricity value, 59 (p.47).

quiz.stem_en: Which substance in the table does NOT fit the pattern 'good heat conductor = good electricity conductor'?
quiz.why_en: Graphite conducts heat well (168) but electricity very poorly (1) (p.47 Q4).

quiz.stem_en: Which of these is a non-metal that CAN conduct electricity?
quiz.why_en: Pencil graphite lights the lamp in the circuit test (p.45-46).

quiz.stem_en: Why are plugs and wire coverings made of plastic or rubber?

choices.en: They are electrical insulators, so electricity cannot reach you

quiz.why_en: Plastic and rubber are electrical insulators (p.61).

quiz.stem_en: Ice melts into water, then the water is put back in the freezer. What kind of change is this?
quiz.why_en: Water can change back to ice — a reversible physical change (p.50).

quiz.stem_en: When a match burns, what does the wood change into?
quiz.why_en: The wood changes into a black substance called carbon (p.50).

quiz.stem_en: Does boiling an egg cause a reversible or irreversible change?

choices.en: Irreversible — the egg cannot go back to raw

quiz.why_en: A cooked egg is a new substance and cannot be changed back (p.50 Q2).

quiz.stem_en: Sort these: which ONE is an irreversible process?
quiz.why_en: Rusting makes a new substance and cannot be reversed; the others are physical changes (p.62 Q3).

quiz.stem_en: In salty sea water, which is the solute and which is the solvent?

choices.en: Salt is the solvent, water is the solute
Salt is the solute, water is the solvent

quiz.why_en: The substance that dissolves is the solute (salt); it dissolves in the solvent (water) (p.51).

quiz.stem_en: Why can't you see the salt after it dissolves in water?

choices.en: The salt particles spread evenly between the water particles
The salt sinks to the bottom

quiz.why_en: Solute particles spread evenly among the solvent particles — the solution looks uniform (p.52).

quiz.stem_en: A solution looks the same all the way through. What word does the book use for this?
quiz.why_en: A solution has a uniform appearance (p.52).

quiz.stem_en: Why did Marcus's coffee taste bitter even though he put in two teaspoons of sugar?

choices.en: He did not stir, so the sugar had not dissolved

quiz.why_en: Without stirring, the sugar stayed at the bottom (p.53).

quiz.stem_en: Name the TWO factors the book says make a solid dissolve faster.

choices.en: Using a bigger jar and more water

quiz.why_en: Stirring and heating both increase the rate of dissolving (p.53-54).

quiz.stem_en: Using the particle model, why does sugar dissolve faster in hot water?

choices.en: Heat gives the particles energy so they move faster and spread out
Sugar particles get smaller in heat

quiz.why_en: Heat adds energy; particles move faster and spread the solute through the solvent more easily (p.54).

quiz.stem_en: Will sugar dissolve in a cup of cold water if nobody stirs it?

choices.en: Only if the cup is metal
Yes, but slowly — particles are always moving

quiz.why_en: Particles in matter are always moving, so it dissolves on its own given time (p.54 Q4).

quiz.stem_en: You put vinegar and bicarbonate of soda in a jar. Which are the reactants?
quiz.why_en: The reactants are the substances that react together (p.57).

quiz.stem_en: Your teacher holds a spoon over a burning candle. Which change is a chemical reaction?
quiz.why_en: Melting and hardening wax are reversible; the burning wick forms new substances (p.56).

quiz.stem_en: Limewater mixed with carbon dioxide forms calcium carbonate. Which is the PRODUCT?
quiz.why_en: Calcium carbonate is the new substance formed (p.59 Q2).

quiz.stem_en: You add cornstarch to water with iodine solution and stir. What evidence of a reaction do you see?
quiz.why_en: The colour changes — investigation A (p.58).

quiz.stem_en: You breathe through a straw into limewater. What do you see, and why?

choices.en: It turns cloudy — carbon dioxide in your breath reacts

quiz.why_en: Carbon dioxide reacts with limewater to make cloudy calcium carbonate (p.58-59).

quiz.stem_en: In investigation B you pour vinegar on wire wool and wait five minutes. What are you measuring?
quiz.why_en: You record the thermometer before and after — a temperature change is evidence (p.59).

quiz.stem_en: Zara drops a fizzy tablet into water. What evidence of a chemical reaction will she see?
quiz.why_en: Gas is produced — one of the signs of a reaction (p.59 Q3).

quiz.stem_en: Boiling water makes bubbles too. Why is that NOT a chemical reaction?

choices.en: Because no new substance forms — the water just becomes a gas

quiz.why_en: Evidence means a PRODUCT has formed. Boiling is a change of state, not a new substance (p.58, p.36).

quiz.stem_en: How well a substance conducts heat is described in the book as what?
quiz.why_en: How well a substance can conduct heat is a property of the substance (p.44).

quiz.stem_en: From the book's table, which substance conducts heat WORST?
quiz.why_en: Steel has the lowest heat value in the table, 80 W/m−K (p.47).

quiz.stem_en: Class 6 put an iron nail in a saucer of water and a few days later it had rusted. What is the product of the reaction?
quiz.why_en: The nail had rusted, so rust is the new substance that formed (p.62 Q5).
